igcse-0580-estimation-rounding-places.description: Choose the closest multiple, round decimal places and show zeros after a carry.

sections.title: Which multiple is nearest?
sections.label: Nearest multiples
sections.intro: Rounding replaces a number with the closest value at a stated place. Mark the two possible results on a number line.

blocks.html: To round to the nearest hundred, compare the two multiples of 100 around the number. For a positive value exactly halfway, choose the greater multiple.

figure.alt: A number line marks 7.28 between 7.2 and 7.3, nearer to 7.3.
figure.caption: \(7.28\) is beyond the halfway point and is closer to \(7.3\).

blocks.title: Find the nearest multiple
blocks.prompt: Round \(1340\) to the nearest \(100\).
blocks.hint: Locate the two multiples on either side before choosing the nearer one.
blocks.solution:
The multiples of 100 on either side are \(1300\) and \(1400\).

\(1340\) is \(40\) above \(1300\) and \(60\) below \(1400\).

The nearer multiple is \(1300\).

blocks.html: Rounding to the nearest hundred is about distance to multiples of 100. It does not always mean moving up.

blocks.title: Round to one decimal place
blocks.prompt: Give the value of \(7.33\) rounded to one decimal place.
blocks.hint: Keep the tenths position and use the hundredths digit to decide whether to round up.
blocks.solution:
The first digit after the point is 3. It is the tenths digit.

The next digit is 3. It tells you whether to raise the tenths digit.

The rounded value is \(7.3\).

blocks.html: Show the place you are rounding to before you inspect the digit immediately to its right.

sections.title: Which digit decides the rounded decimal?
sections.label: Decimal places and halfway
sections.intro: Count places after the decimal point. The first place is tenths and the second is hundredths.

blocks.html: Keep the requested decimal place. Use the next digit to decide if that place increases. One decimal place must still be visible when the last digit is zero.

blocks.title: Round a halfway value
blocks.prompt: Round \(3.145\) to two decimal places.
blocks.hint: Use the third decimal digit. At a positive halfway value, choose the upper multiple.
blocks.solution:
The two nearest hundredths are \(3.14\) and \(3.15\).

\(3.145\) is exactly halfway between them. Its thousandths digit is 5.

For this positive halfway value keep the upper hundredth, \(3.15\).

blocks.html: A carry can increase the ones and leave a zero in the tenths. Write the zero if the question asks for one decimal place.

blocks.title: Show the final zero after a carry
blocks.prompt: Which option shows \(11.968\) correctly rounded to one decimal place?
blocks.hint: A carry across the decimal point can leave zero in the place you are reporting.
blocks.solution:
The tenths digit 9 rises because the next digit is 6.

The change carries into the ones column. The new tenths digit is 0.

One digit after the point must still be shown. Write \(12.0\).

retry.feedback: Your value is close. Count the positions required in the written answer, including zeros after the decimal point.

blocks.html: Use the original number when rounding to a new place. A value that has already been rounded can be misleading.

sections.title: What happens with a carry or a negative number?
sections.label: Carries and negative values
sections.intro: The digit 9 becomes a zero at that place when it carries into the next column. If the number is negative, compare distances to nearby multiples.

blocks.html: Complete the whole-number places with zeros after rounding to tens, hundreds or thousands. For a negative number away from a halfway point, round its magnitude then restore the minus sign.

blocks.title: Carry into the next thousand
blocks.prompt: Round \(5995\) to the nearest hundred.
blocks.hint: The tens digit decides whether the hundreds digit increases.
blocks.solution:
The hundreds digit is 9 and the tens digit is 9.

Rounding up carries from the hundreds into the thousands.

The correct multiple of one hundred is \(6000\).

blocks.html: On the negative side, the nearest value may be further left or further right. Keep the sign when you give the answer.

blocks.title: Use distance for a negative number
blocks.prompt: Round \(-2.17\) to the nearest tenth.
blocks.hint: Compare distances along the number line. The closest position is still negative.
blocks.solution:
Keep the minus sign. Compare the distances to the tenths on either side.

The magnitude \(2.17\) is nearest to \(2.2\).

Reflect back across zero. The answer is \(-2.2\).

blocks.html: For a negative non-halfway value, a short number line can check which marked position is closest.

examples.title: Find the nearest multiple
examples.question: Round \(126\) to the nearest \(10\).
solution: The multiples of 10 on either side are \(120\) and \(130\).
The nearer multiple is \(130\).

examples.title: Round to one decimal place
examples.question: Give the value of \(7.28\) rounded to one decimal place.
solution: The first digit after the point is 2. It is the tenths digit.
The next digit is 8. It tells you whether to raise the tenths digit.
The rounded value is \(7.3\).

examples.title: Round a halfway value
examples.question: Round \(2.815\) to two decimal places.
solution: The two nearest hundredths are \(2.81\) and \(2.82\).
\(2.815\) is exactly halfway between them. Its thousandths digit is 5.
For this positive halfway value keep the upper hundredth, \(2.82\).

examples.title: Show the final zero after a carry
examples.question:
Which option shows \(8.968\) correctly rounded to one decimal place?

A. \(9.0\)   B. \(9\)   C. \(8.9\)   D. \(9.1\)
solution: The tenths digit 9 rises because the next digit is 6.
The change carries into the ones column. The new tenths digit is 0.
One digit after the point must still be shown. Write \(9.0\).

examples.title: Carry into the next thousand
examples.question: Round \(4995\) to the nearest hundred.
solution: The hundreds digit is 9 and the tens digit is 9.
Rounding up carries from the hundreds into the thousands.
The correct multiple of one hundred is \(5000\).

examples.title: Use distance for a negative number
examples.question: Round \(-2.12\) to the nearest tenth.
solution: Keep the minus sign. Compare the distances to the tenths on either side.
The magnitude \(2.12\) is nearest to \(2.1\).
Reflect back across zero. The answer is \(-2.1\).

extraPractice.solution:

extraPractice.hint: Compare distances along the number line. The closest position is still negative.

Keep the minus sign. Compare the distances to the tenths on either side.

The magnitude \(2.22\) is nearest to \(2.2\).

glossary.definition: The size of a digit’s position, such as tens, tenths or hundredths.
A whole number of copies of a chosen unit.
A position counted to the right of the decimal point.
The same distance from the two possible rounded values.
An increase that passes from a place containing 9 to the next place.

revision.body:
Nearest multiples

To round to the nearest hundred, compare the two multiples of 100 around the number. For a positive value exactly halfway, choose the greater multiple.

Decimal places and halfway

Keep the requested decimal place. Use the next digit to decide if that place increases. One decimal place must still be visible when the last digit is zero.

Carries and negative values

Complete the whole-number places with zeros after rounding to tens, hundreds or thousands. For a negative number away from a halfway point, round its magnitude then restore the minus sign.

Example

\(7.28\approx7.3\) to one decimal place.

Check yourself

  • \(6962\) to the nearest hundred.
  • \(12.965\) to one decimal place, with the place shown.

Answers \(7000\) and \(13.0\).
revision.checks:
• Rounding to the nearest hundred is about distance to multiples of 100. It does not always mean moving up.
  • A carry can increase the ones and leave a zero in the tenths. Write the zero if the question asks for one decimal place.
  • On the negative side, the nearest value may be further left or further right. Keep the sign when you give the answer.
revision.examTip: For a negative non-halfway value, a short number line can check which marked position is closest.

igcse-0580-estimation-significant-figure.description: Count from the first non-zero digit and keep the right precision when zeros appear.

sections.title: Where do significant figures start?
sections.label: Find the starting digit
sections.intro: Read left to right until you reach the first non-zero digit. Its position shows the approximate size of the number.

blocks.html: Start counting significant figures there. Digits in places before that do not count. A zero in a later place can count.

figure.alt: A small number is plotted past the halfway mark between 0.0050 and 0.0051.
figure.caption: \(0.00506\) rounds to \(0.0051\) to two significant figures.

blocks.title: Keep the place value of a large number
blocks.prompt: Give the value of \(20332\) correct to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Starting at the first non-zero digit, count the requested number of figures.
blocks.solution:
The first significant digit is the leftmost non-zero digit.

The 3 significant figures bring you to the hundreds place. Check the next digit.

Replace remaining whole-number places with zeros and give \(20300\).

blocks.html: Starting at the decimal point works for decimal places. Significant figures start at the first non-zero digit.

blocks.title: Count a zero after the first non-zero digit
blocks.prompt: Which option gives \(4.0370\) to two significant figures?
blocks.hint: The first significant digit in this number is before the point. The following zero counts.
blocks.solution:
The first significant digit is 4 in the ones place. The next significant digit is 0 in the tenths place.

The hundredths digit is 3. Keep the tenths place unchanged.

Show that two significant figures were retained by writing \(4.0\).

retry.feedback: Your value is close. Count the positions required in the written answer, including zeros after the decimal point.

blocks.html: Underline the first significant digit in your working before counting further.

sections.title: Why do some zeros count and others stay as placeholders?
sections.label: Zeros and carries
sections.intro: Leading zeros show the position of a small number. A zero after the first significant digit can record accuracy.

blocks.html: When a carry changes the leading position, check the significant figures in the written answer again. For example, \(0.00996\) to two significant figures is \(0.010\).

blocks.title: Find the first non-zero digit in a small number
blocks.prompt: Which option gives \(0.0003534\) to three significant figures?
blocks.hint: Count from the first non-zero digit, even if it appears several places after the point.
blocks.solution:
Ignore the zeros that come before the first non-zero digit when counting significant figures.

Count three digits from the first non-zero digit. Use the fourth significant digit to round.

Keep the leading zeros in their places and write \(0.000353\).

blocks.html: Dropping the last zero in \(0.010\) would leave only one significant figure visible.

blocks.title: Keep two figures when rounding changes the leading place
blocks.prompt: Which option shows \(0.0009960\) rounded to two significant figures?
blocks.hint: After the carry, find the new first significant digit. Count two figures in the result.
blocks.solution:
The digit after the first two significant digits requires rounding up.

Both retained 9s carry. The first significant digit moves one place left.

Show the two significant figures of the result by writing \(0.0010\).

retry.feedback: Your value is close. Count the positions required in the written answer, including zeros after the decimal point.

blocks.html: Keep the number the same size as the original. Add any required leading, trailing or whole-place zeros.

sections.title: Which kind of accuracy is the question asking for?
sections.label: Choose a starting point
sections.intro: Underline the instruction. Count decimal places from the point and significant figures from the first non-zero digit.

blocks.html: The same number can round to different results under these two instructions. Check your final answer against the required unit and accuracy.

blocks.title: Compare decimal places with significant figures
blocks.prompt: Round \(5.02374\) to two decimal places and to two significant figures. Which pair gives the answers in that order?
blocks.hint: Read the first instruction from the decimal point and the second from the first non-zero digit.
blocks.solution:
For decimal places, count two places after the point. The result is \(5.02\).

For significant figures, start with the ones digit 5. The second significant place is the tenths.

The ordered pair of answers is \(5.02\) and \(5.0\).

field.label: Value to two decimal places and value to two significant figures

blocks.html: Two decimal places and two significant figures often need different digits even when there is only one digit before the point.

blocks.title: Use one significant figure for a value below one
blocks.prompt: Write the value of \(0.747\) correct to one significant figure.
blocks.hint: Do not count the zeros before the first non-zero digit.
blocks.solution:
The first significant digit is the first non-zero digit.

Use the following digit to decide whether this digit stays or increases.

The rounded value is \(0.7\).

blocks.html: Use the requested accuracy. Where a result is not exact and the question gives no instruction, the 0580 convention is normally three significant figures, with angles in degrees given to one decimal place.

examples.title: Keep the place value of a large number
examples.question: Give the value of \(18213\) correct to 2 significant figures.
solution: The first significant digit is the leftmost non-zero digit.
The 2 significant figures bring you to the thousands place. Check the next digit.
Replace remaining whole-number places with zeros and give \(18000\).

examples.title: Count a zero after the first non-zero digit
examples.question:
Which option gives \(3.0370\) to two significant figures?

A. \(3.0\)   B. \(3\)   C. \(3.04\)   D. \(3.1\)
solution: The first significant digit is 3 in the ones place. The next significant digit is 0 in the tenths place.
The hundredths digit is 3. Keep the tenths place unchanged.
Show that two significant figures were retained by writing \(3.0\).

examples.title: Find the first non-zero digit in a small number
examples.question:
Which option gives \(0.003527\) to three significant figures?

A. \(0.00353\)   B. \(0.004\)   C. \(0.0035\)
solution: Ignore the zeros that come before the first non-zero digit when counting significant figures.
Count three digits from the first non-zero digit. Use the fourth significant digit to round.
Keep the leading zeros in their places and write \(0.00353\).

examples.title: Keep two figures when rounding changes the leading place
examples.question:
Which option shows \(0.009960\) rounded to two significant figures?

A. \(0.010\)   B. \(0.01\)   C. \(0.0100\)   D. \(0.011\)
solution: The digit after the first two significant digits requires rounding up.
Both retained 9s carry. The first significant digit moves one place left.
Show the two significant figures of the result by writing \(0.010\).

examples.title: Compare decimal places with significant figures
examples.question:
Round \(4.02374\) to two decimal places and to two significant figures. Which pair gives the answers in that order?

A. \(4.02\) and \(4.0\)   B. \(4.0\) and \(4.02\)   C. \(4.03\) and \(4.0\)   D. \(4.02\) and \(4.1\)
solution: For decimal places, count two places after the point. The result is \(4.02\).
For significant figures, start with the ones digit 4. The second significant place is the tenths.
The ordered pair of answers is \(4.02\) and \(4.0\).

examples.title: Use one significant figure for a value below one
examples.question: Write the value of \(0.743\) correct to one significant figure.
solution: The first significant digit is the first non-zero digit.
Use the following digit to decide whether this digit stays or increases.
The rounded value is \(0.7\).

A zero before the first non-zero digit. It holds a position but does not count.
A zero written at the end of a decimal can show the reported accuracy.
The level of detail used to state a result.
A zero that keeps the other digits in their correct places.

igcse-0580-estimation-estimate-calculati.description: Round inputs to convenient values, keep the operations and check the size of the result.

sections.title: When does the rounding happen?
sections.label: Round the inputs
sections.intro: An estimate is an approximate answer that you can work out quickly. Replace the original inputs by nearby values before calculating.

blocks.html: If the question asks for one significant figure, round each input separately. Use \(\approx\) for the step where you replace an expression by an estimate.

figure.alt: Three rows with ten dots in each illustrate thirty as a rough product.
figure.caption: With rounded inputs of \(10\) and \(3\), the estimate contains three groups of ten.

blocks.title: Round both addends before adding
blocks.prompt: Estimate \(32.4+1.86\) by rounding each value to one significant figure.
blocks.hint: Round the two original values first, then carry out the addition.

blocks.html: Rounding the exact answer afterward does not show how the estimate was obtained.

blocks.title: Estimate a product
blocks.prompt: By rounding each value to one significant figure, estimate \(9.90\times 3.55\).
blocks.hint: The estimate uses the product of the two rounded inputs, not the rounded exact output.
blocks.solution:
\(9.90\) is approximately \(10\). \(3.55\) is approximately \(4\).

Multiply the rounded numbers. \(10\times 4=40\).

The estimate for the original product is \(40\).

blocks.html: Write the rounded expression as a full line of working. Then evaluate that expression.

sections.title: How do I keep the calculation sensible?
sections.label: Preserve groups and divisors
sections.intro: Use the same operations in the same order as the original. The fraction bar groups the whole numerator and the whole denominator.

blocks.html: Round a non-zero small divisor by significant figures, rather than changing it to zero by rounding to a whole number. If a rounded denominator still becomes zero, the proposed estimate does not work.

blocks.title: Keep an estimated divisor non-zero
blocks.prompt: Estimate \(\frac{1.508}{0.49}\) by rounding each value to one significant figure.
blocks.hint: Do not round a decimal divisor to the nearest whole number when the question asks for one significant figure.
blocks.solution:
The rounded numerator is \(2\) and the rounded denominator is \(0.5\).

The denominator has one significant figure even though its whole-number digit is zero.

Calculate \(\frac{2}{0.5}\), which equals \(4\).

blocks.html: A zero in the ones place does not mean the decimal has no significant digits.

blocks.title: Keep the fraction bar and bracket structure
blocks.prompt: Round each number to one significant figure, then estimate \(\frac{46.1+12.5}{2.21\times 4.88}\).
blocks.hint: Round the four written values individually. Keep the addition in the numerator and multiplication in the denominator.
blocks.solution:
The rounded calculation is \(\frac{50+10}{2\times 5}\).

The numerator is \(60\) and the denominator is \(10\).

The estimate is \(6\).

blocks.html: Once the inputs have been rounded, calculate with them. The same group stays under a square-root bar.

sections.title: How can I estimate a root and check the scale?
sections.label: Check the scale
sections.intro: Keep the entire rounded group inside a square root. Use the estimate to spot a misplaced decimal point or an order-of-operations error.

blocks.html: Show enough working to see why an answer close to 120 is plausible when the estimate is 120. An answer near 12 or 1200 deserves another check.

blocks.title: Estimate before evaluating a square root
blocks.prompt: Round each number inside \(\sqrt{4.19\times 8.80}\) to one significant figure. Then estimate the root.
blocks.hint: Keep the square-root bar over the full rounded product.
blocks.solution:
The rounded values are \(4\) and \(9\).

Multiply inside the root first. The rounded product is \(36\).

The positive square root is \(6\).

blocks.html: An estimate can flag a possible error. It does not prove that an exact answer is correct.

blocks.title: Check the scale of a calculator result
blocks.prompt: What is the most plausible estimate of \(39.9\times 2.99\)? Round both inputs to one significant figure.
blocks.hint: Use a rough product to choose its scale. Check it against the positions of the decimal points.
blocks.solution:
\(39.9\) is close to \(40\) and \(2.99\) is close to \(3\).

The rough product is \(40\times 3=120\).

An answer a factor of 10 away is on the wrong scale for this calculation.

blocks.html: Keep the full calculator value in working when you later need an accurate result.

examples.title: Round both addends before adding
examples.question: Estimate \(28.7+1.81\) by rounding each value to one significant figure.
solution: The estimate is \(32\).

examples.title: Estimate a product
examples.question: By rounding each value to one significant figure, estimate \(9.82\times 3.24\).
solution: \(9.82\) is approximately \(10\). \(3.24\) is approximately \(3\).
Multiply the rounded numbers. \(10\times 3=30\).
The estimate for the original product is \(30\).

examples.title: Keep an estimated divisor non-zero
examples.question: Estimate \(\frac{0.408}{0.21}\) by rounding each value to one significant figure.
solution: The rounded numerator is \(0.4\) and the rounded denominator is \(0.2\).
The denominator has one significant figure even though its whole-number digit is zero.
Calculate \(\frac{0.4}{0.2}\), which equals \(2\).

examples.title: Keep the fraction bar and bracket structure
examples.question: Round each number to one significant figure, then estimate \(\frac{43.8+11.2}{2.12\times 4.84}\).
solution: The rounded calculation is \(\frac{40+10}{2\times 5}\).
The numerator is \(50\) and the denominator is \(10\).
The estimate is \(5\).

examples.title: Estimate before evaluating a square root
examples.question: Round each number inside \(\sqrt{4.18\times 8.80}\) to one significant figure. Then estimate the root.
solution: The rounded values are \(4\) and \(9\).
Multiply inside the root first. The rounded product is \(36\).
The positive square root is \(6\).

examples.title: Check the scale of a calculator result
examples.question:
What is the most plausible estimate of \(38.9\times 2.95\)? Round both inputs to one significant figure.

A. \(12\)   B. \(120\)   C. \(1200\)
solution: \(38.9\) is close to \(40\) and \(2.95\) is close to \(3\).
The rough product is \(40\times 3=120\).
An answer a factor of 10 away is on the wrong scale for this calculation.

extraPractice.hint: Round the two original values first, then carry out the addition.

extraPractice.hint: The estimate uses the product of the two rounded inputs, not the rounded exact output.

Multiply the rounded numbers. \(10\times 4=40\).

extraPractice.prompt: Estimate \(\frac{0.808}{0.21}\) by rounding each value to one significant figure.
extraPractice.hint: Do not round a decimal divisor to the nearest whole number when the question asks for one significant figure.
extraPractice.solution:
The rounded numerator is \(0.8\) and the rounded denominator is \(0.2\).

The denominator has one significant figure even though its whole-number digit is zero.

Calculate \(\frac{0.8}{0.2}\), which equals \(4\).

extraPractice.title: Keep the fraction bar and bracket structure
extraPractice.prompt: Round each number to one significant figure, then estimate \(\frac{48.4+13.8}{2.30\times 4.92}\).
extraPractice.hint: Round the four written values individually. Keep the addition in the numerator and multiplication in the denominator.
extraPractice.solution:
The rounded calculation is \(\frac{50+10}{2\times 5}\).

The numerator is \(60\) and the denominator is \(10\).

The estimate is \(6\).

extraPractice.title: Estimate before evaluating a square root
extraPractice.prompt: Round each number inside \(\sqrt{4.20\times 8.80}\) to one significant figure. Then estimate the root.
extraPractice.hint: Keep the square-root bar over the full rounded product.
extraPractice.solution:
The rounded values are \(4\) and \(9\).

Multiply inside the root first. The rounded product is \(36\).

The positive square root is \(6\).

extraPractice.title: Check the scale of a calculator result
extraPractice.prompt: What is the most plausible estimate of \(40.9\times 3.03\)? Round both inputs to one significant figure.
extraPractice.hint: Use a rough product to choose its scale. Check it against the positions of the decimal points.
extraPractice.solution:
\(40.9\) is close to \(40\) and \(3.03\) is close to \(3\).

The rough product is \(40\times 3=120\).

An answer a factor of 10 away is on the wrong scale for this calculation.

glossary.definition: An approximate value found by a quicker calculation.
A number that was present before the calculation.
The number by which you divide.
On a sensible scale for the original calculation.
The symbol \(\approx\) means approximately equal to.

revision.body:
Round the inputs

If the question asks for one significant figure, round each input separately. Use \(\approx\) for the step where you replace an expression by an estimate.

Preserve groups and divisors

Round a non-zero small divisor by significant figures, rather than changing it to zero by rounding to a whole number. If a rounded denominator still becomes zero, the proposed estimate does not work.

Check the scale

Show enough working to see why an answer close to 120 is plausible when the estimate is 120. An answer near 12 or 1200 deserves another check.

Example

\(9.82\times3.24\approx 10\times3=30\).

Check yourself

  • Estimate \(\frac{1.62}{0.21}\) using one significant figure per input.
  • Estimate \(\frac{43.8+11.2}{2.12\times4.84}\) in the same way.

Answers \(\frac{2}{0.2}=10\). \(\frac{40+10}{2\times5}=5\).
revision.checks:
• Rounding the exact answer afterward does not show how the estimate was obtained.
  • A zero in the ones place does not mean the decimal has no significant digits.
  • An estimate can flag a possible error. It does not prove that an exact answer is correct.
revision.examTip: Keep the full calculator value in working when you later need an accurate result.

igcse-0580-estimation-appropriate-accura.description: Decide whether a real situation needs a nearest value, an extra container or a count of complete groups.

sections.title: When should a result move up or down?
sections.label: Whole groups
sections.intro: A quotient can leave a remainder. Ask what the remainder means in the situation before choosing the whole-number answer.

blocks.html: Round up when every item needs a place and another group may be partly full. Round down when only complete items or groups count.

figure.alt: Three groups each contain four counters. A fourth group contains the thirteenth counter.
figure.caption: Thirteen items need four containers that each fit four items. Only three full groups can be made.

blocks.title: Round up when every item needs a place
blocks.prompt: A studio packs 32 model boats. Each crate holds at most 5 boats. What is the minimum number of crates needed?
blocks.hint: The answer must provide a place for every boat. Check what happens to the remainder.
blocks.solution:
6 full crates hold 30 boats.

There are 2 boats left. They need one more crate even though it will not be full.

The minimum is 7 crates.

retry.feedback: That many crates only fit the full groups. Put the remaining boats in one more crate.

blocks.html: Rounding to the nearest whole number can undercount the containers you need or overcount the items you can cut.

blocks.title: Round down when only complete pieces count
blocks.prompt: A roll of fabric is 30 metres long. Each banner needs 4 metres and joining offcuts is not allowed. How many complete banners can be cut?
blocks.hint: Count only full lengths. Check whether the remaining fabric is long enough for another banner.
blocks.solution:
7 banners use 28 metres.

The remaining 2 metres is shorter than one full banner.

The roll supplies 7 complete banners.

retry.feedback: One extra banner would require more fabric than the roll contains.

blocks.html: Show what fits in the complete groups, then test what remains.

sections.title: Which position matches the units?
sections.label: Precision from the units
sections.intro: Choose a place that answers the question in the required units. One centimetre is one hundredth of a metre.

blocks.html: Record a price to the nearest penny using two decimal places in pounds. If the requested final position is zero, keep it visible.

blocks.title: Report money to the nearest penny
blocks.prompt: A price calculation gives £\(4.2975\) before rounding. Which option records the price correctly to the nearest penny?
blocks.hint: One penny is one hundredth of a pound. Keep the pence position visible.
blocks.solution:
The pounds and pence display needs two digits after the decimal point.

The hundredths digit rounds up, because the next digit is 7. The carry gives \(4.30\).

The price is £\(4.30\).

retry.feedback: Your value is close. Count the positions required in the written answer, including zeros after the decimal point.

blocks.html: Keep the units in the result. Copying the same digits with a different unit changes the stated quantity.

blocks.title: Choose the place for a measured length
blocks.prompt: A track length is \(3.305\,\mathrm m\). Record its value in metres correct to the nearest centimetre.
blocks.hint: Keep working in metres. A centimetre corresponds to the second decimal place.
blocks.solution:
One centimetre is \(0.01\,\mathrm m\). Work in hundredths of a metre.

Use the thousandths digit of \(3.305\) to decide which hundredth is nearer.

The recorded length is \(3.31\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: When the question states a degree of accuracy, use it in place of the usual exam convention.

sections.title: What do I report when the question gives no extra rule?
sections.label: Final accuracy
sections.intro: Keep the calculation accurate until the end. Use estimates early only when a question asks for a rough result or you want to check the scale.

blocks.html: Unless told otherwise, Cambridge 0580 uses three significant figures for non-exact numerical answers and one decimal place for angles in degrees.

blocks.title: Report an angle using the exam convention
blocks.prompt: A calculator gives an angle of \(6.87383^\circ\). The question gives no other required accuracy. Which displayed value follows the 0580 convention?
blocks.hint: The default for angles in degrees differs from the default for other non-exact numerical answers.
blocks.solution:
In 0580, use one decimal place for a non-exact angle in degrees unless the question specifies otherwise.

The first decimal place is the tenths position. Use the next digit to round.

Report \(6.9^\circ\).

blocks.html: Rounding intermediate results can shift the final answer. Keep the unrounded result when it feeds another part.

blocks.title: Keep extra working digits and round the final value
blocks.prompt: A calculator gives a non-exact length of \(2.090231\,\mathrm m\). No accuracy is specified. Which final value follows the 0580 convention?
blocks.hint: Count from the first non-zero digit. The question asks for the final value rather than the number used in the working.
blocks.solution:
For a non-exact numerical answer other than an angle in degrees, the default here is three significant figures.

The calculator value has more digits than required. Keep the full value in working and take the fourth significant digit when rounding.

The final reported value is \(2.09\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: Report the final answer to the right accuracy and include the correct units.

revision.body:
Whole groups

Round up when every item needs a place and another group may be partly full. Round down when only complete items or groups count.

Precision from the units

Record a price to the nearest penny using two decimal places in pounds. If the requested final position is zero, keep it visible.

Final accuracy

Unless told otherwise, Cambridge 0580 uses three significant figures for non-exact numerical answers and one decimal place for angles in degrees.

Example

With 13 items and four spaces per container, fill three containers. The final item needs a fourth container.

Check yourself

  • A box holds eight cups. How many boxes are needed for 34 cups?
  • Report a non-exact angle of \(42.785^\circ\) using the usual 0580 precision.

Answers Five boxes. \(42.8^\circ\).
revision.checks:
• Rounding to the nearest whole number can undercount the containers you need or overcount the items you can cut.
  • Keep the units in the result. Copying the same digits with a different unit changes the stated quantity.
  • Rounding intermediate results can shift the final answer. Keep the unrounded result when it feeds another part.
revision.examTip: Report the final answer to the right accuracy and include the correct units.
